candidates.quote: What do we live for, if it is not to make life less difficult to each other?
candidates.author: George Eliot
candidates.speaker: Dorothea Brooke
candidates.whyThisMonth: The whole case for kindness put as a plain question, asked by the character who lives it, and short enough to carry into the day.

candidates.quote: There is no charm equal to tenderness of heart.
candidates.author: Jane Austen
candidates.locator: Volume II, chapter 13 (chapter 31 in continuous numbering)
candidates.speaker: Emma Woodhouse, to herself
candidates.whyThisMonth: Emma, the cleverest person in her village, concedes at last that warmth beats cleverness, which is a good thing to concede before breakfast.

candidates.quote: Life appears to me too short to be spent in nursing animosity or registering wrongs.
candidates.author: Charlotte Brontë
candidates.speaker: Helen Burns
candidates.whyThisMonth: Helen Burns answers Jane’s appetite for grievance with the one sentence that lets a grudge go before the day starts.

candidates.quote: There is no religion without love, and people may talk as much as they like about their religion, but if it does not teach them to be good and kind to man and beast it is all a sham.
candidates.author: Anna Sewell
candidates.locator: Part I, chapter 13, The Devil’s Trade Mark
candidates.speaker: John Manly
candidates.whyThisMonth: The circle widened to include the animals, in the plainest voice in the book: kindness is the test, and everything else is talk.

candidates.quote: You never really understand a person until you consider things from his point of view … until you climb into his skin and walk around in it.
candidates.author: Harper Lee
candidates.speaker: Atticus Finch, to Scout
candidates.whyThisMonth: The novel’s founding instruction in compassion, given to a child at bedtime and just as usable at six in the morning.

candidates.quote: She is a friend of my mind. She gather me, man. The pieces I am, she gather them and give them back to me in all the right order.
candidates.author: Toni Morrison
candidates.speaker: Sixo, remembered by Paul D
candidates.whyThisMonth: The best description in American fiction of what one person can do for another, and a picture of the friend to be today.

candidates.quote: As far as the education of children is concerned I think they should be taught not the little virtues but the great ones. Not thrift but generosity and an indifference to money; not caution but courage and a contempt for danger; not shrewdness but frankness and a love of truth; not tact but love for one’s neighbour and self-denial; not a desire for success but a desire to be and to know.
candidates.author: Natalia Ginzburg
candidates.whyThisMonth: Generosity and love of one’s neighbour set above thrift and tact: the opening of the essay is a whole morning’s worth of what to teach and what to be.

candidates.quote: Ultimately, we have just one moral duty: to reclaim large areas of peace in ourselves, more and more peace, and to reflect it toward others.
candidates.author: Etty Hillesum
candidates.work: An Interrupted Life: The Diaries of Etty Hillesum 1941 to 1943
candidates.whyThisMonth: Kindness traced back to its source: make peace in yourself first, then give it away, which is a morning practice in one sentence.

candidates.quote: I feel at home in the entire world, wherever there are clouds and birds and human tears.
candidates.author: Rosa Luxemburg
candidates.work: Letter to Mathilde Wurm, Wronke prison, 16 February 1917
candidates.locator: The Letters of Rosa Luxemburg, ed. Adler, Hudis and Laschitza (Verso, 2011), p. 376
candidates.whyThisMonth: Written from a prison cell, a refusal to keep compassion for one corner of the world only: the circle drawn as wide as it goes.

candidates.quote: Mankind was my business. The common welfare was my business; charity, mercy, forbearance, and benevolence, were, all, my business.
candidates.author: Charles Dickens
candidates.speaker: Jacob Marley’s Ghost
candidates.whyThisMonth: The most famous correction in English fiction of what a day’s business actually is, useful before the day’s business begins.

candidates.quote: Compassion is the chief law of human existence.
candidates.author: Fyodor Dostoevsky
candidates.speaker: Prince Myshkin, in thought
candidates.whyThisMonth: The month’s theme stated as a law by the one character in Dostoevsky who keeps it, in eight words that fit a card.

candidates.quote: Let the tears of the poor man find with thee more compassion, but not more justice, than the pleadings of the rich.
candidates.author: Miguel de Cervantes
candidates.speaker: Don Quixote, counselling Sancho Panza before he governs his island
candidates.whyThisMonth: Compassion with its eyes open: the knight’s counsel to a new governor is advice for anyone who will judge somebody today.

candidates.quote: If a man should importune me to give a reason why I loved him, I find it could no otherwise be expressed, than by making answer: because it was he, because it was I.
candidates.author: Michel de Montaigne
candidates.locator: Book I, chapter 27, Of Friendship (chapter 28 in modern numbering)
candidates.whyThisMonth: The sentence the essay is known by: affection that needs no reason, which is the ground every act of kindness stands on.
candidates.translator: Charles Cotton, ed. W. C. Hazlitt, 1877

candidates.quote: There is a land of the living and a land of the dead and the bridge is love, the only survival, the only meaning.
candidates.author: Thornton Wilder
candidates.work: The Bridge of San Luis Rey
candidates.locator: Part Five, Perhaps an Intention, closing sentence
candidates.speaker: The Abbess, Madre María del Pilar, in thought
candidates.whyThisMonth: The closing line of the novel gives love the last word over loss, and sends the reader out to be somebody’s bridge.

candidates.quote: I have learnt that all men live not by care for themselves but by love.
candidates.author: Leo Tolstoy
candidates.locator: Section XII, the angel’s closing speech
candidates.speaker: The angel Michael
candidates.whyThisMonth: The moral of the tale in a single line: the stranger taken in from the cold was the point all along.

candidates.quote: You become responsible, forever, for what you have tamed.
candidates.author: Antoine de Saint-Exupéry
candidates.speaker: The fox
candidates.whyThisMonth: The fox’s rule turns affection into obligation: whoever you have let close is yours to look after today.

curatorNotes.verification: Web access was available. Wording checked against the Project Gutenberg plain texts (downloaded and grepped) for: Eliot (#145, ch. LXXII), Austen (#158, Volume II ch. XIII), C. Brontë (#1260, ch. VI), Sewell (#271, ch. 13), Cervantes Ormsby (#996, Part II ch. XLII), Montaigne Cotton (#3600, Book I ch. XXVII), Dostoevsky Eva Martin (#2638, Part II ch. V), Dickens (#46, Stave One), Tolstoy Maude (#6157, section XII). Wilder, Morrison, Ginzburg, Hillesum, Luxemburg, Lee and Saint-Exupéry were checked against web sources only; see the per-line hedges.

hedges.02-fict-04: Gutenberg text reads: said John; there is no religion without love ... to man and beast it is all a sham--all a sham, James, and it won’t stand when things come to be turned inside out. The proposal capitalises the first word and stops at the dash; the verifier should decide whether the cut is acceptable.
hedges.02-fict-05: In the text Scout interrupts with Sir? between point of view and until; the ellipsis marks that omission. The uncut fallback is the first clause alone, ending at point of view.
hedges.02-fict-06: Page numbers from the Knopf first edition are from memory (pp. 272 to 273, the Paul D and Sethe scene near the end of Part Three) and should be checked; the line is Sixo’s, remembered by Paul D, so the reporter goes in the note.
hedges.02-fict-07: Two online transcriptions of the Davis translation differ on one word in the third clause: not shrewdness (Christian Science Monitor review, 1986) versus nor shrewdness (a blog). The proposal follows the 1986 review. Davis’s translation appeared in 1985 (Carcanet, UK; Seaver, US); a 2017 Arcade reissue puts the passage at p. 121.
hedges.02-fict-08: The diary date of 29 September 1942 comes from secondary sources, not from the page itself; the English is Pomerans’s (Cape/Pantheon 1983, Holt 1996 reissue). The UK printing may read towards others; the US printing reads toward others. Page not located.
hedges.02-fict-09: Wording and page from a scholarly article citing the Verso 2011 Letters (trans. George Shriver), p. 376. The older Bronner edition (1978) drops the comma after world. Luxemburg was born in Russian Poland and wrote in German from Berlin; country given as Germany.
hedges.02-fict-11: Eva Martin’s 1913 rendering is verified verbatim. Other translations differ: Garnett has the longer chief and perhaps the only law form. Dostoevsky already has one line in the year (month 1); this would be his second of three.
hedges.02-fict-01: George Eliot already has one line in the year (month 1); this would be her second of three.
hedges.02-fict-13: Cotton’s Book I numbers this essay 27; modern editions (Frame, Screech) number it 28. Frame’s 1957 wording differs: If you press me to tell why I loved him, I feel that this cannot be expressed, except by answering: Because it was he, because it was I.
hedges.02-fict-16: The Woods wording is as given on Wikiquote and in the standard 1943 Reynal and Hitchcock edition from memory; Richard Howard’s 2000 translation differs (You’re responsible for your rose). Checked against the Wikiquote page, not the printed book.
